en: The Biography of Bodhisattva Deva, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Bodhisattva Deva was a native of South India and a disciple of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna. He was...
He was of the Brahmin caste.
His learning was vast and his grasp profound;
his talent and eloquence were peerless.
Renowned throughout India, he was highly esteemed by all nations;
having thoroughly explored the depths of his own mind, he felt no shame.
His sole concern was that which remained unfinished: the worry that people would not place their trust in his words.
In that country there was a great celestial deity;
a golden image of him was cast, two zhang in height, seated upon a throne,
and was called Maheśvara.
There was a person who sought a boon that might be fulfilled in this present life.
Deva went to the temple to enter and pay his respects.
The master of the temple said:
The celestial image is a supreme deity; those who behold it dare not gaze upon it directly, and it causes people to lose their composure for a hundred days after they have retreated.
You need only go there to inquire and seek your wishes; why must you see it?
Devadatta said: "If the Self were necessarily as you describe it, then let me see it alone.
If it is not so, how could it be something I wish to see?"
The people of the time marveled at his resolute spirit and were humbled by his brilliant integrity;
those who followed him into the temple numbered several million.
Once Deva had entered the temple, he...
The deity moved its eyes and glared at him with a wrathful gaze.
Deva asked the deity, "If you are truly a god, why are you so small?
You ought to move people through your majestic spirit and subdue things through your wisdom and virtue."
Yet he falsely used gold to make himself appear more numerous;
by moving the crystal, he caused confusion regarding what was not expected.
He then immediately climbed a ladder and gouged out its eyes.
At that time, all the onlookers harbored doubts,
wondering why Maheśvara had been so humiliated by a single minor brāhmaṇa;
they feared that his reputation exceeded his actual merit and that he was now reduced to silence by the exhaustion of his arguments.
Deva informed the multitude that the divine spirit was far-reaching and vast;
therefore, he tested me with mundane matters.
Having grasped his intention, I ascended the mountain of gold and brought forth crystal.
"I have caused you to know that the spirit does not depend on matter and the essence does not rely on form.
Since I do not treat the spirit with arrogance, the spirit likewise does not bring me shame.
Having said this, he departed.
That very night, he prepared all the necessary offerings.
At dawn the following day, he reverently made sacrifices to the heavenly deities.
Since Deva’s reputation was already great, his wisdom further accorded with the divine.
Whenever he uttered a word, wherever his voice reached, there was no response that did not arise.
Within a single night, all manner of refined delicacies for offerings were prepared, with every requisite item provided.
Mahādeva [appeared] impaled upon a single human corpse, reaching a height of several dozen *zhang*.
His left eye was withered and dry when he came and took his seat;
surveying the offerings all around, he marveled at their unprecedented excellence and praised the power of his virtue for having brought them about.
He addressed him, saying: "You have grasped my mind.
Others grasp my form, whereas you offer me your mind; others present material gifts, whereas you know how to provide for me through understanding.
Those who revere me do so out of awe, while those who slander me are merely people. As for the food you have provided, it is indeed excellent and exquisite."
"Only that which is required by one who is without self can be truly considered a supreme gift for one who is able to give.
Deva said, "Your divine insight perceives my heart; I shall follow your command.
The deity said, "That which I lack is my left eye. If you are able to give it to me, you may extract it."
Devadatta said, "I honor you as if obeying a divine command," and immediately with his left hand he plucked out an eye and gave it to him.
By the power of the deity, as soon as it was removed, another grew in its place.
He demanded them without ceasing from dawn until the end of the day, until tens of thousands of eyes had been produced.
The deva praised him, saying:
"Excellent, Māṇava! This is a truly supreme gift.
Whatever wish you seek, it shall surely be fulfilled according to your heart's desire."
Deva said, "I have received clear instruction regarding the mind; it does not depend on external things.
My only regret is that the common folk are so ignorant that they do not know to believe and accept my words."
"O Divine One, grant me my wish; you must surely cause my words not to be in vain.
This alone is my request; I require nothing else.
The Divine One replied, "It shall certainly be as you have wished."
Thereupon, he withdrew to visit Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna,
received the dharma of renunciation, shaved his head, donned the monastic robes, and traveled about to propagate the teachings.
At that time, the King of South India ruled over all the various states and followed heterodox paths with full confidence.
Not a single person among the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, was able to see him.
People from near and far throughout the country were all transformed by his Way.
Deva thought to himself:
If a tree does not have its root cut down, its branches will not fall.
If the ruler does not transform [the people], the Way will not be practiced.
In that state, the government established a system where the royal house provided funds to hire men for night watch and guard duty.
Deva then accepted the recruitment to serve as their general;
he took up his halberd to lead the vanguard,
rectifying the ranks and disciplining the units.
His authority was effective without severity,
and all things joyfully followed him without his virtue being ostentatiously displayed.
The King was greatly pleased and asked who this person was.
The attendant replied, "This man responded to the call for volunteers;
he neither eats from the granary nor takes money,
yet his conduct in these matters is so respectful, diligent, and well-practiced."
Not knowing his intention— what he sought or what he desired—
the king summoned him and asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am an omniscient one."
The King was greatly startled and questioned him, saying:
"A person of all-encompassing wisdom appears but once in many generations.
You claim this for yourself; by what means may it be verified?"
He replied, "If you wish to know, wisdom lies in speaking;
Your Majesty should question me.
The king then thought to himself, "I am the master of wisdom and a great master of debate."
If he can be made to yield when questioned, it is still not enough to be called a victory.
Once he fails to do so, it is no small matter.
If he does not yield upon being questioned, that itself constitutes a defeat.
He remained in doubt for a long time.
Unable to bear it any longer, he asked, "What is the Deva doing now?
Tīva replied, "The Deva is currently at war with the asuras."
When the King heard these words, he was like a person choking: unable to spit it out and unable to swallow it down.
If he wished to reject the words, there was no means to prove them false;
yet if he wished to accept the matter, there was nothing to clarify it.
Before he had finished speaking,
Deva spoke again:
"This is not empty talk nor words sought for the sake of victory."
Wang Xiaodai waited for a short while and the proof was manifest.
As soon as he finished speaking, dryads and weapons began to descend from the air;
long halberds and short blades fell down in continuous succession.
The king said, "Although spears, halberds, lances, and pikes are indeed weapons of war,
why must you know that this was a battle between the devas and the asuras?
Devala replied, "These are but empty words."
"It would be better to verify this with actual facts.
Having spoken, the asura’s hands, feet, fingers, ears, and nose descended from the sky.
The king then prostrated himself, submitting to his spiritual transformation.
In the palace hall, there were ten thousand brahmins,
all of whom discarded their topknots and received the precepts of accomplishment.
At that time, Deva established a high seat within the royal capital and set forth the Three Treatises.
It is said that among all holy ones, the Buddha is the most supreme;
among all dharmas, the Buddha-dharma is truly the foremost; and among all saviors of the world, the Buddha and the Sangha are the first.
If there were any debaters from the eight directions capable of refuting these words,
I would cut off my head to atone for my defeat. Why is this?
To have an unclear understanding of principles is ignorance.
I have no need for the head of one who is ignorant;
I would rather cut it off to atone for my defeat, for I do not begrudge it.
When the scholars from the eight directions heard these words, they also each assembled there and made this vow:
"We shall likewise sever our own heads;
we cannot bear to be inferior to him."
I do not even begrudge my own foolish head.
Deva said, "The Dharma I practice brings life to all things;
it must surely be superior."
"I shall shave off your hair and beard to make you my disciple;
there is no need to cut off your head.
Having established this agreement, each composed their own systematic principles and constructed boundless treatises.
In engaging in such exchanges,
those of shallow wisdom and limited capacity would be defeated by a single word,
while those of deep wisdom and long-standing character would continue for as long as two days.
Consequently, their arguments and reasoning were both exhausted,
and they all shaved their heads.
In this manner, day after day, the royal household sent ten carts of robes and alms bowls until it was finally finished.
In the third month, more than one million people were delivered [to liberation].
Among them was a disciple of a heterodox path who was cruel, obstinate, and devoid of wisdom;
though he followed the multitude, he felt ashamed that his master had humbled himself.
Bound by resentment and anger in his heart, he bit down on a blade and made this vow:
"Since you have overcome me with your mouth,
I shall overcome you with my sword."
"You have distressed me with a sword of emptiness;
I shall distress you with a sword of reality.
Having made this vow, he gripped a sharp blade and waited for an opportunity.
The eminent masters and heroes of all quarters were completely exhausted [in debate].
Thereupon, Āryadeva retired to a secluded grove and composed the *Śataśāstra* in twenty chapters.
Furthermore, he composed the *Catuḥśataka* to refute false views.
His disciples were each sitting in meditation and contemplation beneath various trees.
Deva arose from his meditation and began to walk in circumambulation (*caṅkrama*).
A disciple of the brahmin came to his side, took up a sword, and threatened him, saying:
"You have destroyed my teacher with your words; how about I destroy your belly with this sword?"
He immediately cut open [the man's] belly with a knife, and his five viscera lay scattered upon the ground;
while the man’s life was not yet extinguished, [the Buddha], out of pity for this foolish thief, addressed him, saying:
"I have my three robes and alms bowl here at my seat; you may take them."
Hurry up and go up the mountain; be careful not to descend to the level road below.
My disciples who have not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyānakṣānti) will surely seize you, or they will capture you and deliver you to the authorities.
The king will then oppress you, and you will not yet have attained the benefits of the Dharma.
To cherish the body is a heavy attachment; to cherish fame is likewise so called.
From both body and name, afflictions and entanglements arise.
From this, manifold afflictions arise.
That which constitutes one's body and name is the very root of great suffering.
The ignorant, lacking learning, are assailed by false views.
To regret what one should not regret,
while failing to regret what one ought to regret—
is this not truly lamentable?
I have received the Bequeathed Dharma of the Buddha and am no longer like that.
I only think of how you have been deceived by your own deranged minds and scorched by the fires of anger and venom,
such that the retribution for your sins has not yet ceased.
They received it while wailing and sobbing;
yet those who received it truly had no master,
and those who performed it truly had no agent.
"Without a person and without a master,
this pitiless thing— who could seek it out through reality?
It cannot be found in reality."
Those who have not yet awakened to this are deluded by a frantic mind;
they are turned about by inversion and become attached to what they perceive as the attainment of the heart-mind.
Yet there is a self, there are persons, and there is suffering and pleasure.
The arising of suffering and pleasure depends solely upon contact;
when one is free from attachment, there is no longer any dependence.
Without dependence, there is no suffering;
without suffering, there is no pleasure.
When both suffering and pleasure are absent, one is nearly at rest.
Having spoken these words, the disciple who had arrived first let out a piercing cry.
The disciples gathered one by one from among the forest trees;
those who had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyānakṣānti) were struck with terror and wailed aloud, beating their breasts and striking the ground.
"Alas! What a tragedy! Who has taken my teacher in such a manner?
Some rushed forward in a frantic charge, intercepting him on the main road;
they divided into groups and pursued him with cries that deafened the deep valleys.
Devadatta instructed the people, saying: "Regarding the reality of all phenomena (*dharmas*), who is the enemy?
Who is the cruel one? Who cuts? Who severs?
In the reality of all phenomena, there is truly no experiencer and no harmer."
"Who is your friend? Who is your enemy? Who is your thief?
Who is your hater? You have been deceived by the poison of delusion;
you have falsely given rise to views of attachment and wailed aloud, planting seeds of unwholesome karma."
"What that person has harmed is the retribution of his own karma; he has not harmed me.
You all should reflect on this and be careful not to pursue madness with madness; rather, mourn with a compassionate sorrow.

Thereupon, he cast off his body, becoming liberated and free from all attachment, and departed like a cicada shedding its shell. As he first emerged, his eyes and spirit were gone; thus, he was left without a single eye.
The people of that time called him Kanadeva.
